az_buffalo_park.blurb: A small bouldering area on the east side of a city park in Flagstaff, on coarse, gritty basalt. Small cliff bands and scattered blocks hold low-ball problems, slabs, cracks and a few taller faces, with most problems falling between VB and V4 and a handful much harder. Centerpiece and Block Arete are favorite moderates, and Block Roof and Willful Unconsciousness give stronger climbers something to chew on. The rock is sharp on the skin and holds are plentiful, so lines are often loosely defined. Landings vary, so bring a pad, and expect hikers, riders and runners passing nearby on the park trails.
az_buffalo_park.parking_note: Use the large lot off Gemini Drive on the north edge of the park, then walk in on foot.
az_buffalo_park.approach: A short hike from the lot past the large green water tank, then a social trail along the south side of the fence and down through a gap in the cliff band; under five minutes.

az_the_right_wall.blurb: The right-hand side of The Waterfall, a basalt amphitheater in Oak Creek Canyon north of Sedona. The wall is mostly vertical and technical, with thin cracks, small crimps and gas-bubble pockets that make smooth-looking rock climbable, so it rewards careful gear placement while moving. Nearly all of it is trad, and the grades sit mainly in the 5.11 and 5.12 range with a few easier warm-ups on the margin. It faces west, which brings morning shade and afternoon sun. Rockfall is a real concern, especially in cold wet spells and monsoon storms, so wear a helmet at the base. A 70 m rope and a full rack with multiple small cams are worth carrying.
az_the_right_wall.parking_note: The small roadside pullout on a bend of Highway 89A holds only a handful of cars; the nearby Encinoso day-use area is the usual backup.
az_the_right_wall.approach: Cross Oak Creek and work upstream through a drainage of boulders and roots to the main amphitheater, keeping the falls on your left as you face it. Plan on 30 to 45 minutes. High water can make the crossing difficult, especially in early spring.

az_middle_section.blurb: The central stretch of cliffs on Granite Mountain outside Prescott, known for long crack and face lines on pale, fine-grained stone. Most climbs are traditional and run two to five pitches, with grades spread mainly from 5.8 through 5.11 and a few harder test pieces; The Classic is a popular moderate. The approach is a good hike on the wilderness trail followed by a faint climbers' path, so allow a real morning or day. Descent is usually by rappel, and the first rappel is long, so check your rope length before committing. Spring and fall tend to give the steadiest weather.
az_middle_section.parking_note: Start from the Metate trailhead in Granite Basin: take Iron Springs Road northwest of Prescott, turn onto Granite Basin Road and follow it to the Metate lot on the left.
az_middle_section.approach: Follow Trail 261 about 1.7 miles to a green metal gate, keep right on the switchbacks, and watch for a big patch of prickly pear near the second large switchback, where the faint climbers' path to the wall leaves the trail (roughly 2 miles total).

az_wall_of_the_trundling_trolls.blurb: A crack-split wall in the Munchkinland zone of Mount Lemmon, across a canyon from the Dancing Dwarfs, with compact, very solid rock and few loose holds. Most climbs are trad on crack systems with gear every few feet, plus a handful of bolted face routes between the cracks. Grades cluster in the 5.9 to 5.11 range, and Business as Usual and Valhalla are among the better-known lines. A stream runs nearly all year at the base, though it should be filtered before drinking. Water can seep from the upper left part of the wall after rain, and summer storms arrive fast. It cools off quickly in late fall.
az_wall_of_the_trundling_trolls.parking_note: Drive to the end of Rose Canyon Road and use one of the large lots above the lake; there is roadside room when they fill.
az_wall_of_the_trundling_trolls.approach: Take the trail that starts behind the snack bar at Rose Canyon Lake, climb to the Munchkinland ridgeline, drop to the Dwarfs wall, and continue down a faint trail into the bottom of upper Sycamore Canyon; under 10 minutes below Munchkinland. Trees often fall across the path.

az_beardsley_roped_routes.blurb: The roped climbs among the big granite boulders on a desert hill in north Phoenix. Coarse, weathered desert granite makes for grippy, durable rock, and the larger formations above the main boulder field carry a mix of trad, some bolted sport lines and a couple of top-rope setups. Grades run from easy fifth class up through the 5.10s, with 5.9 and 5.10 the most common. It is a short, convenient outing, good for an evening or a quick lead practice session, and the same hillside has plenty of bouldering. Snake Pit Arête is the standout sport line, and The Flake makes a simple top-rope.
az_beardsley_roped_routes.parking_note: From Cave Creek Road, turn onto Lone Cactus Road and follow it to the dead-end lot; it is small, so a handful of cars fills it.
az_beardsley_roped_routes.approach: Walk northwest from the lot, roughly a third of a mile, toward the hillside you can see ahead.

az_finland_terrace.blurb: One of the first walls reached on the upper trail at The Homestead, a remote desert canyon of steep limestone sport climbing in Gila County. Finland Terrace is all bolted, with tufa-streaked faces and a grade spread that favors the 5.11s and 5.12s, plus a few moderates; Masterpiece Theater and Radical Self Expression are favorites. It sits next to Tufa City and the Finland sections along the west side of the canyon. A 70 m rope and a full set of quickdraws help. The area is best in the cool half of the year, and summer heat and thunderstorms can be harsh.
az_finland_terrace.parking_note: Turn east off Highway 77 roughly 16 miles south of Globe onto the rough dirt road and follow it to the upper trailhead and camping area. High clearance helps; a low car can stop earlier and walk the road.
az_finland_terrace.approach: From the trailhead kiosk, walk about 0.4 mile to the crag trail, then take the left fork uphill; the Terrace is the first section along it.

az_rappel_rock_2.blurb: A high-elevation formation near the top of Mount Lemmon above Tucson, where temperatures stay cooler than in the desert below. The faces are mostly south-facing and carry a good number of longer, moderate trad climbs, with a smaller number on the east and north sides; Chiboni and Black Quacker are well-known routes. Most grades fall between 5.7 and 5.11, with 5.8 through 5.10 the most common. Boulders scattered around the summit area add bouldering from easy to very hard. The routes were established long ago and can feel stiff for their grade. The final approach follows a steep, cairned climbers' trail.
az_rappel_rock_2.parking_note: Take the Catalina Highway toward Summerhaven and turn right toward the ski valley, then follow the narrow paved road up to the observatory area, where there is a gravel lot and some roadside room.
az_rappel_rock_2.approach: From the observatory, take the trail left of the fenced antennas to the Mt. Lemmon Trail #5 left fork, walk about 15 minutes, then take the cairned climbers' trail downhill on the left to the back of the rock.

az_slate_nation.blurb: A sport wall at The Homestead, a remote limestone canyon in Gila County, reachable from either of the two main trails. Every route is bolted, and the grades concentrate in the 5.11 and 5.12 range, with a few moderate warm-ups and a couple of 5.13s, so it suits climbers who are already comfortable on steep, technical limestone. Clean Slate and Infectious Groove are worth seeking out. The canyon is remote and very hot in summer, which makes the cooler months the better time. Bring a 70 m rope and plenty of draws.
az_slate_nation.parking_note: Turn east off Highway 77 about 16 miles south of Globe onto a rough dirt road and follow it to the upper trailhead and camping area. High clearance helps; a low car can park earlier and walk.
az_slate_nation.approach: From the trailhead, hike about 0.4 mile to the crag trail; the wall can be reached by either the left or right trail.

az_hall_of_legends_mid_leap.blurb: A deep, steep cleft in the middle of the Apache Leap cliff band above Superior, with long, exposed multi-pitch sport climbing on welded volcanic tuff. The walls rise several hundred feet and the routes run from two to six pitches, mostly in the 5.9 to 5.11 range, with Ussen and Child of Water among the best known. Expect an adventurous feel: bring a 70 m rope, 20 or more quickdraws and a helmet, as there is some loose rock in the notch. It is a long hike to reach, and descents are by rappel or the one-pitch escape route, so plan on a full day.
az_hall_of_legends_mid_leap.parking_note: Use the small lot at the end of Magma Mine Road, short of the mine gate, and continue on foot.
az_hall_of_legends_mid_leap.approach: Follow cairns and a dirt trail across drainages and over ridges toward the cleft; about 45 minutes to an hour.

az_sun_spot_crags.blurb: A low, south-facing cliff band above Molino Campground on the lower Catalina Highway on Mount Lemmon, popular as a sunny, warm winter crag. Climbs are a mix of bolted sport lines and trad routes on cracks and chimneys, with grades mainly in the 5.10 and 5.11 range and a few easier and harder ones. Rock quality varies, but the lines are better than they look from below, and Solar Flare on the far west end has especially good stone. The short approach makes it a quick outing, though the sun can be punishing once temperatures climb in the warm months. Bring a standard trad rack for the crack lines.
az_sun_spot_crags.parking_note: Use the Molino Campground lot, a short distance up the highway from the entrance station.
az_sun_spot_crags.approach: Cross the road to the Arizona Trail heading east, walk a minute or two, then leave it up the hillside to the north past an abandoned mine; about 15 minutes.

_conflicts.az_rappel_rock_2: rock: none stored; Lemmon is gneiss per climbing.com but Rappel Rock page silent; not added
